Heracles, called Hercules by the Romans. The strongest man who ever lived, and the illegitimate son of Zeus and the mortal woman Alcmene. Famous above all for completing the Twelve Labors—a series of seemingly impossible tasks that represent the archetype of the hero who achieves immortality through suffering and perseverance.

His life began under a curse. Hera, the jealous wife of Zeus, persecuted him relentlessly throughout his mortal years, sending him trials and madness itself. As an infant, she sent two serpents to murder him in his cradle, but the baby Heracles strangled them with his bare hands, foreshadowing the superhuman strength that would define him.

His great works of redemption arose from his greatest tragedy. Hera sent him a madness that drove him to kill his own wife and children. When the madness cleared and he understood what he had done, only one path to redemption remained open. He was assigned the Twelve Labors, a series of tasks so difficult that they were thought to be impossible for any mortal.

His first labor was to slay the Nemean Lion, whose hide could not be pierced by any weapon. Heracles strangled it with his bare hands and wore its pelt as armor for the rest of his life, the lion's head serving as a helmet. His second labor was to defeat the Lernaean Hydra, a many-headed serpent that grew two new heads for each one that was cut off. Heracles solved the problem by cauterizing each stump with fire to prevent regrowth, slaying the monster through cunning as much as strength.

The labors continued. He captured the Golden Hind of Artemis, retrieved the girdle of the Amazon queen, and captured the Erymanthian Boar. In his final and most dangerous labor, he descended to the Underworld and brought back Cerberus, the three-headed guard dog that kept the dead from escaping. He even cleansed the Augean Stables, a task that seemed literally impossible, in a single day.

After his labors ended, Heracles married Deianeira, a princess who loved him deeply. But she was deceived by a dying centaur into giving Heracles a robe she believed to be magical. In truth, it was soaked in the poisoned blood of the Centaur Nessus, and when Heracles wore it, the poison burned his flesh with agony beyond endurance. Unable to bear the suffering, he chose to end his torment by mounting a funeral pyre. As he burned, his immortal part ascended to Olympus, and he was transformed into a god.

In the divine realm, he finally found peace. He married Hebe, the goddess of youth, and joined the Olympians as a full immortal. Heracles is central to Western heroic tradition precisely because he earned his divinity through struggle rather than inheriting it. His journey from mortal suffering to divine transcendence became the template for how heroes should endure.
